newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Clinton aide sought campaign funds in Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Clinton aide sought campaign funds in Taiwan.

text.p: A former White House aide who travelled to Taiwan last year clearly told his hosts he had come to raise money for President Bill Clinton, the Washington Post reported on Wednesday.
It is against the law for foreigners to contribute to U.S. political campaigns.

Chen Yu-chun, the political scientist who worked as the campaign spokesman for Taiwanese presidential candidate Lin Yang-king before last March's elections, told the paper Mark Middleton's purpose was clear, but he never directly asked for a contribution.

"Mr. Middleton mentioned that the reason he came to Taiwan was to raise money for Clinton," Chen told the paper. "He did not tell us how much money he wanted. But he said if Mr. Lin wanted to go to the White House, he could make all the arrangements."
Chen said Lin's campaign never contributed to the Clinton campaign.

The U.S. Justice Department is investigating reports that another Clinton administration official, James Wood Jr., an Arkansas lawyer whom Clinton appointed as chief U.S. liaison with Taiwan, was engaged in fundraising for the Democratic National Committee in Taiwan.

The reports have surfaced amid scrutiny of the DNC's fundraising activities and criticism from Republicans over the Democrats' acceptance of contributions from foreign interests seeking influence with the administration.

The Post noted that Chen's comments were particularly puzzling since the DNC and the Clinton/Gore campaign have issued statements saying Middleton had no direct or indirect money-raising duties in the 1996 campaign.

Middleton, 34, is an Arkansas native who was one of the first volunteers for Clinton in 1991. In 1992, the Post said, he played a key role raising funds for Clinton and was rewarded with a job as deputy to then-White House Chief of Staff Mack McLarty.

While in Taiwan last summer, Middleton also met with Liu Tai-ying, the head of the business arm of Taiwan's ruling party, laying the groundwork for a subsequent encounter between Clinton and Liu at a fundraiser in San Francisco, a senior administration official told the Post.
